newsitem.title: UK: Force for Zaire: saviour or dangerous gamble?.
newsitem.headline: Force for Zaire: saviour or dangerous gamble?.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Driven by conscience and enormous pressure to act, Western powers have finally decided to send troops to Zaire on a mission that could either help save the starving or turn into a disaster of epic proportions.

Tough questions have yet to be answered on the force's humanitarian mandate and responsibilities, and on how much it can really do to help the turmoil in Central Africa. A political solution to the problems of the region seems as distant as ever.

The heavy fighting that erupted around the town of Goma on Thursday underlined the risks of military entanglement with rebels or Hutu fighters, potentially a major threat to American, British, French and other soldiers a long way from home.

The United States, Britain and France have made clear there are no plans for the multinational force, which is to be led by Canada and could number more than 10,000 troops, to disarm the powerful Hutu militia established in eastern Zaire.
The problem, many aid officials say, is that if this is not done it will be impossible to distribute food, water and medicine properly.
Diplomats say most countries are reluctant to risk casualties by pushing for anything other than a humanitarian mission to deliver aid, to be given official blessing by the U.N. Security Council.

That is particularly true of the United States, which led the ill-fated U.N. mission in Somalia in 1993. President Bill Clinton, fresh from his election triumph, has agreed only reluctantly to take part in the Zaire operation.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Thursday the operation would be strictly humanitarian. But the potential for another ill-defined, hasty mission clearly worries Western governments, which cannot afford another disaster on the scale of previous U.N. operations in Bosnia and Somalia.
In both instances, troops on a humanitarian mission were sent into a chaotic region where there was no ceasefire and little prospect of one -- as is the case in Zaire.
"There are still a lot of unanswered questions about the wider issues," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday. "But that should not be a cause for delay."
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry promised there would have to be "clarity of mission" before Washington would give a final commitment to send its troops.
In practice, diplomats say, it would be hard for any Western power to back out now and watch thousands of people die in graphic television coverage beamed around the world by satellite.

Besides, the wheels are in already in motion and the pressure to act seems irresistible. France, which has led the drive to send troops, said on Thursday it hoped the first soldiers would arrive in the region this weekend.

The multinational force will have long and difficult lines of supply and communication and it is not yet clear under what circumstances it will be able to use force in a confused situation where Hutu militia, the Zairean army and Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels have all been fighting.
Aid agencies say more than one million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi are widely scattered, making it difficult to find and reach them.
Beyond the practicalities, there are also wider questions about the wisdom of the mission.
France and Britain, former colonial powers in Africa, have decided to take part although they are viewed with suspicion by countries in the region like Uganda and Rwanda.
Rwanda has accused France of supporting the Hutus blamed for the 1994 genocide in which an estimated 800,000 people, mainly Tutsis, were slaughtered.

Many of the Hutus responsible fled subsequently to eastern Zaire. Washington and its allies do not want to feed and give sanctuary to the well-armed Hutu militia that is now in place and frustrating efforts to get Rwandan refugees to go home.
But, unless the multinational force takes on the militia, diplomats say, it is unclear how much aid will get to the people who most need it.
